records.query: What can I make with pasta, cheese and peas? My son is 3.
records.response:
Lovely — peas, cheese and pasta: the holy trinity of toddler comfort food. Quick, low-drama ideas your three-year-old will probably eat without staging a sit-in.

Short list — pick one:

1) Creamy pea & cheese pasta (one-pot, ~20 min)
- Method: boil pasta; add frozen peas last 2–3 min, drain, stir in a splash of milk and 2–3 tbsp grated cheese until creamy.
- Toddler tweaks: minimal/no salt; mash a few peas if texture is an issue.
- Portion: ~½ cup cooked pasta + ¼ cup peas + 2–3 tbsp sauce.
- Freezing: ok for 1–2 months; reheat gently, add splash of milk if separated.

2) Cheesy pea pasta bake (25–30 min)
- Method: mix pre-cooked pasta + peas + mild cheese sauce, top with breadcrumbs, bake 15–20 min.
- Toddler tweaks: cool and cut into small squares; smooth sauce so no lumps.
- Portion: ~½ cup per child.
- Make-ahead: freeze assembled or baked portions; reheat covered.

3) Pasta bites (mini muffin tin, 15–20 min)
- Method: mix pasta, peas and cheese, press into mini muffin tins; chill or bake 8–10 min to set.
- Toddler tweaks: finger-friendly pieces — cut small; avoid big shells.
- Portion: 3–4 small bites ≈ ½ cup total.
- Freezing: freeze individual bites, reheat from frozen.

4) Lemon-butter pea pasta with optional ham (15–18 min)
- Method: toss cooked pasta + peas with a knob of butter, small squeeze of lemon; add tiny diced ham if wanted.
- Toddler tweaks: very little salt; finely dice ham to avoid choking.
- Portion: ~½ cup pasta + ¼ cup peas + 2–3 tsp sauce.
- Best fresh (lemon doesn’t freeze well).

records.query: My toddler has a high temperature, what should I do?
records.response:
I’m sorry — that’s worrying. Follow this NHS guidance now:

Immediate actions
- Keep them comfortably cool: remove extra layers and avoid wrapping them up.
- Offer plenty of fluids regularly (small, frequent sips).
- If they seem very uncomfortable, you can consider an age-appropriate over-the-counter child pain/fever medicine. Follow the NHS/packet advice exactly or ask a pharmacist.
- Check on them regularly through the night if it’s bedtime.

Do NOT
- Do not sponge them with cold water or put them in a cold bath.
- Do not over- or under-dress them.
- Do not give any medicines that are not specifically suitable for their age/weight.
- Do not give any adult medicines. If unsure, ask a pharmacist.
- Do not give anti-inflammatory medicines to babies under 3 months or under 5 kg.
- Never give medicines containing salicylates to under-16s.

Go to hospital now (A&E) or call 999 if any of the following
- They are under 3 months and have a temperature of 38°C or higher.
- They are 3–6 months and have a temperature of 39°C or higher.
- Fever with a stiff neck or sensitivity to light.
- Fever with a rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it.
- They have a fit or seizure for the first time.
- They are unusually cold to touch, very sleepy, floppy, or hard to wake.
- You’re very worried they are seriously unwell.

Call NHS 111 for urgent advice if
- They are under 2 years old and the fever lasts more than 24 hours.
- They are 2 years or older and the fever lasts more than 3 days.
- You’re worried or need advice, but it’s not an emergency.

If you’re unsure about medicine dosing, contact a pharmacist or call 111. If at any point you think they’re seriously unwell, call 999 straight away.

NHS source: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/baby/health/treating-a-high-temperature-in-children/

records.query: What do I do if my child is choking?
records.response:
You’re right to ask — choking is scary. Follow this NHS guidance exactly.

Immediate actions
- If they’re coughing and able to breathe/talk: encourage them to keep coughing. Stay with them and watch closely.
- If they cannot cough, cry or breathe: call 999 immediately.
- For a child aged 1 or over:
  - Give up to 5 back blows: stand or kneel behind them, support their chest with one hand, lean them forward, and hit firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
  - Still choking? Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, place a fist just above the belly button (below the ribs), grasp with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
  - Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or help arrives.
- For a baby under 1:
  - Give up to 5 back blows: lay baby face down along your forearm with their head lower than their body; support the head and neck; give firm blows between the shoulder blades.
  - Still choking? Give up to 5 chest thrusts: turn baby face up, with head lower than body; place 2 fingers in the middle of the chest just below the nipple line and push down sharply up to 5 times.
  - Alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until relieved or help arrives.
- If they become unresponsive at any point: call 999 and start CPR if you’re able, following the call handler’s instructions.

Do NOT
- Do not put your fingers in their mouth to “sweep” the object (you can push it further in).
- Do not hold them upside down.

When to go to hospital (A&E) or call 999
- Call 999 if they can’t breathe, cough or cry, or if choking is ongoing.
- Go to hospital after a choking episode even if the object seems to have cleared, to check for any damage.
- If abdominal thrusts were used, they must be seen due to risk of internal injury.
- If you think something is still stuck.

Call NHS 111 if
- They had a choking episode but seem fine now and you want clinical advice.
- They have a persistent cough or ongoing symptoms after the episode.

This is NHS guidance. If they’re currently unable to breathe, call 999 now. If you’re unsure but they’re breathing, call 111 for advice or contact your GP. Consider booking a paediatric first-aid course so you feel prepared next time.

records.query: My child touched the hob and burnt their hand.
records.response:
I’m sorry this has happened — stay calm. Do this immediately:

What to do now (start straight away)
- Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes. Start as soon as possible.  
- Remove jewellery and any tight clothing near the burn (for a hand: remove rings/wristbands) unless stuck to the skin.  
- Keep your child warm while you cool the burn (wrap them in a coat/blanket, but keep the burn under running water).  
- After 20 minutes of cooling, cover the burn loosely with cling film (lay it lengthways in strips) or a clean, non‑fluffy dressing or plastic bag.  
- For pain, you may use age‑appropriate pain relief if advised by a pharmacist or NHS 111.

Do NOT
- Do not use ice or iced water.  
- Do not put creams, butter, toothpaste, or powders on the burn.  
- Do not burst blisters.  
- Do not remove clothing that is stuck to the burn.  
- Do not use fluffy materials like cotton wool directly on the burn.

Go to hospital (A&E) now
- Burns on the hand should be assessed in hospital. After first aid, go to A&E now.  
- Also go to A&E if any of the following apply:
  - The burn is bigger than your child’s hand.  
  - The skin looks white, charred, leathery, or the burn seems deep.  
  - It’s very painful even after 20 minutes of cooling.  
  - The burn goes all the way around the limb.  
  - It’s a chemical or electrical burn.  
  - For babies and toddlers, any burn should be seen even if small.

Call NHS 111 for urgent advice if
- The burn is small and superficial on a non‑sensitive area and you’re unsure about care.  
- You need advice on dressings or suitable pain relief.

Call 999 (emergency) if
- Your child is very unwell, faint, unusually drowsy, or you cannot get to A&E safely and quickly.  
- You suspect a large or deep burn and there’s any concern about their overall condition.

Follow‑up care
- Keep the burn covered with cling film or a clean, non‑fluffy dressing as advised by the clinician.  
- Do not burst blisters or pick scabs.  
- Watch for signs of infection: increasing redness or swelling, warmth, pus, fever, worsening pain, or a bad smell — seek medical advice (GP/111/A&E) if these occur.  
- Protect healing skin from the sun.  
- If you’re unsure at any point, contact NHS 111 or your GP for advice.

records.query: Since my son Max turned 2 last week he's been really fussy with food.

Ah — the second birthday: when toddlers discover the word “no” and apply it to dinner. Totally normal, stressful, and annoying in equal measure. I’ve saved Max (age 2) to your profile so I’ll remember this next time you ask for reinforcements.

Quick why (two-minute science)
- New independence + testing boundaries = refusing food to show control.
- Appetite swings: growth spurts mean feast one day, famine the next.
- Neophobia: suspicious of new textures/flavours after big changes.
- Routine helps — predictability calms toddlers.

What to try right now (low-drama, actually works)
- Keep mealtimes calm and short (20–30 mins). No screens. Eat together if you can.
- One familiar + one tiny new bite per meal. No force, no bribes, neutral praise.
- Small portions: think 2–4 tbsp per item for a 2‑year‑old. Let them ask for more.
- Snack schedule, not grazing: 2–3 snacks a day, 2–3 hours from meals.
- Milk: aim ~350 ml/day so it doesn’t replace meals. Offer water between meals.
- Prep hacks: batch-cook bases (rice/pasta/mash), freeze portions, hide veg in sauces.

Five go-to, quick toddler meals
- Veggie omelette fingers + toast
- Chicken + (sweet) potato mash with peas
- Tuna mayo wrap (cucumber strips)
- Pasta with tomato + grated veg (dairy-free cheese optional)
- Hummus + veggie sticks + fruit

3‑day sample plan (short)

- Day 2: Scrambled egg on toast; banana; lentil soup; dairy-free yogurt; salmon fish cakes + broccoli
- Day 3: Dairy-free yogurt + granola; pear; pasta with tomato-veg sauce; pitta+hummus; veggie fried rice + egg

- Protein: eggs, canned tuna, chicken, lentils, salmon/fish cakes
- Staples: oats, pasta, rice, wraps, passata, hummus, dairy-free yogurt/cheese if needed

- Check on them regularly, including overnight.

Do NOT
- Do not assume a rash is “just viral” without doing the glass test.
- Do not wait if the rash does not fade with a glass — call 999.
- Do not use cold baths, cold sponging or fans; just keep the room cool and clothing light.
- Do not give any medicine that isn’t specifically for children and age-appropriate, or without advice from a pharmacist/GP/111.

- Go to hospital urgently if your baby is under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, or 3–6 months with a temperature of 39°C or higher.

Call NHS 111 if
- Your child has a rash with a mild fever but seems otherwise well and you want advice on care at home.
- The rash lasts more than a few days, or you’re unsure what type of rash it is.
- The temperature lasts more than 24 hours in a child under 2, or more than 3 days in a child over 2.
- You’re worried at any point, even if they don’t seem seriously unwell.

records.query: My 4 year old has had a cough for 3 days, should I be worried?
records.response:
You’re doing the right thing checking — it’s normal to worry. Short answer: probably not urgent, but watch for the red flags below.

Immediate actions now (NHS-based)
- Keep them comfortable and well hydrated: offer small, frequent sips of fluids.
- Let them rest; quiet play is fine if they feel up to it.
- If the cough is worse at night, try propping their head and shoulders up when they’re awake and supervised.
- For a blocked/runny nose, saline nasal drops/spray can help clear mucus.
- For children over 1 year, a warm drink with honey and lemon can soothe a sore throat and cough.
- Keep the room cool and well-ventilated; avoid stuffy, overheated rooms.
- Watch their breathing: look for fast breathing, working hard to breathe (tummy sucking in under the ribs, flaring nostrils, grunting), or struggling to speak/eat because of breathlessness.

Do NOT
- Do not give over-the-counter cough or cold medicines or decongestants to children under 6 unless a pharmacist/doctor advises it.
- Do not use steam inhalation (risk of burns and no proven benefit).
- Do not give honey to children under 1 year (your child is 4, so honey is fine).
- Do not expose them to tobacco smoke or vaping aerosols.
- Do not delay seeking urgent help if breathing becomes difficult or they seem very unwell.

Go to A&E or call 999 now if any of these happen
- Severe breathing difficulty: struggling to breathe, cannot speak in short sentences, ribs/neck pulling in with breaths, noisy breathing at rest (stridor), grunting, or they can’t catch their breath.
- Skin, lips or tongue look blue, pale or grey.
- They are very drowsy, hard to wake, floppy, or not responding as usual.
- A non-blanching rash (does not fade when you press a glass on it) with fever.
- They cough and choke repeatedly or there’s a large amount of blood in the cough.
- You’re seriously concerned they are acutely unwell.

Call NHS 111 urgently if
- You think it might be croup: a barking cough, hoarse voice, and a harsh noise when breathing in (stridor) — especially if it’s getting worse.
- They have signs of breathing difficulty but not severe (breathing faster than usual, mild pulling-in under ribs, wheeze).
- A high temperature and they feel very unwell or the fever is not settling with self-care.
- They are not drinking enough, have fewer wet nappies/peeing much less, or show signs of dehydration (dry mouth, no tears when crying).
- They have chest pain, are unusually sleepy/irritable, or you’re worried about how they look or behave.
- The cough is getting worse, is waking them persistently at night, or they have repeated coughing fits with vomiting.

See your GP (non-urgent appointment) if
- The cough lasts longer than 3 weeks.
- The cough keeps coming back, or they’re getting frequent chest infections.
- There’s persistent wheeze, ongoing night cough, or you’re concerned about asthma-type symptoms.
- They have a long-term condition (for example affecting the heart, lungs, or immunity) and you’re worried about how the cough is affecting them.

Typical duration
- Most coughs from colds/viral infections improve within 1 to 3 weeks. It’s common for a child’s cough to last up to 3 weeks after a cold.

Self-care that helps (NHS advice)
- Fluids often; offer regular small drinks.
- Rest and comfort.
- Warm fluids; for children over 1, honey in a warm drink can soothe.
- Saline nasal drops/spray for a blocked nose.
- Keep the home smoke-free; fresh air and a comfortable, cool room can help.
- If they seem uncomfortable or feverish, you can consider age-appropriate pain/fever relief — a pharmacist can advise what’s suitable for a 4-year-old.

Next step
- If any breathing problems or the severe signs above appear, call 999 now.
- If you’re worried but it’s not an emergency, call NHS 111 for advice.
- Otherwise monitor and use the self-care above; book a GP if the cough lasts more than 3 weeks or gets worse.

records.query: Something to help my 4 year old with counting, about 20 minutes.
records.response:
Nice. Twenty minutes is a beautiful, achievable amount of chaos. Here’s a quick, ready-now session to boost counting skills—no special kit, minimal bribery.

What you need (2 minutes to grab)
- 10–20 small objects (cars, socks, grapes, Lego, toy animals)
- A bowl or box
- A piece of paper and pen (or sticky notes)
- Space for a short hop or walk

20-minute plan (easy to follow)
1. Warm-up — Counting together (3 mins)
   - Line up 10 toys. Count them aloud together, pointing to each one. Model steady pace and one-to-one matching (“one, two, three…”).
2. Main game — Treasure Hunt + Count (10 mins)
   - Hide objects around a room (5–12 depending on ability). Give child the bowl.
   - They find and put each object in the bowl, counting as they add: “One… two… three.”
   - When finished, count all aloud together and write the number on a sticky note and stick it to the bowl.
   - Repeat, but this time ask “How many if we add two more?” (show two more objects and count on from the total).
3. Quick challenge — Number Line Jump (4 mins)
   - Tape numbers 1–10 (or 1–20) on the floor. Call a number and they jump to it, shouting the number and counting there if needed.
   - Mix it up: “Jump to 5, then count to 8 from there” to practise counting on.
4. Cooldown — Praise and mini-record (3 mins)
   - Ask them to pick a favourite number and tell you why. Praise effort. Note one thing they did well (e.g., “Great pointing for each toy!”).

Alternative 20-minute swaps (pick one if that sounds better)
- Snack Maths: Give 12 crackers/berries. Count them, share into two plates, count again — simple dividing and subtraction practice.
- Toy Train Sort: Make trains of 3, 4, 5 cars. Count cars per train and compare which is more/less.
- Story Count: Read a short story and count repeated objects (e.g., 7 ducks in the pond).

Quick tips that actually work
- One-to-one is king: point and count each item. Don’t let them guess.
- Praise attempts, not just correct numbers.
- If they skip or lose place, gently model again: “Let’s point together.”
- Keep sessions fun and short — end on success.

records.query: How do I know if a bump on the head is serious?
records.response:
Sorry you’re worried — stay calm. Follow this NHS guidance:

Immediate actions now
- Sit them down, keep them calm and resting. Avoid rough play for the rest of the day.
- Hold something cold (e.g., frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel) on the bump for up to 10 minutes at a time to reduce swelling.
- Observe them closely for the first few hours. Try to keep them awake initially so you can monitor how they are.
- If it’s sleep time, it’s OK to let them sleep, but check them regularly. Make sure they rouse and respond normally when you check.
- If there’s a cut that’s bleeding, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth. If bleeding does not stop, go to A&E.

Do NOT
- Do not leave them unmonitored for the first few hours.
- Do not shake them to keep them awake.
- Do not return them to climbing, running, cycling, scooters or sports the same day.
- Do not give any medicines unless advised by a healthcare professional. If you think pain relief is needed, ask a pharmacist, call NHS 111, or speak to your GP.

Go to hospital (A&E) or call 999 now if any of the following happen
- They were knocked out or unconscious, even briefly.
- They vomit more than once after the injury.
- A seizure or fit.
- Clear fluid or blood coming from the ears or nose.
- They’re unusually drowsy, hard to wake, or not responding normally.
- Problems with vision, walking, balance or coordination.
- Weakness or numbness in arms or legs.
- Bruising behind the ears or around the eyes not due to a direct hit.
- A fall from a significant height (more than their own height).
- Any head bump in a baby under 1 year.

Call NHS 111 or your GP urgently if
- You’re worried but they seem otherwise OK.
- Headache that does not go away or is getting worse.
- A very large bump or swelling that’s not improving after a few days.
- They’ve vomited once but are otherwise well.
- You notice changes in behaviour (more irritable, not themselves), or they’re more sleepy than usual, but not severely.

Watchful waiting and recovery
- Watch closely for 24–48 hours. If any red-flag symptoms develop, go to A&E or call 999.
- Let them rest. Quiet activities only for 24–48 hours; no sports, climbing frames, bikes or scooters until fully well.
- It’s normal for a small bump to be sore and swollen for a couple of days. Swelling should gradually go down.
- If symptoms (such as headache, irritability, trouble concentrating) persist beyond 2 weeks, arrange a GP review.

If you’re unsure at any point, call 111 for urgent advice, or 999 in an emergency. If you want, tell me the child’s age and what happened and I’ll help you decide the next step.

records.query: My son has a high fever, a stiff neck and a rash that won't fade when I press a glass on it - what illness has he got?
records.response:
You’re right to be worried — those are red‑flag signs. Call 999 now.

Why: A high fever plus a stiff neck and a rash that does not fade when pressed (non‑blanching) are signs that could indicate meningitis or sepsis. This is an emergency.

Immediate actions (do these now)
- Call 999 now and say: “child with non‑blanching rash and fever; possible meningitis.”
- Stay with your child and follow the call handler’s instructions.
- If needed, repeat the glass test (press a clear glass firmly on the rash). If it doesn’t fade, that supports the need for emergency help.
- Note when the rash began and whether it’s spreading; take a clear photo for paramedics.
- Keep your child comfortable: remove extra layers if hot, or cover lightly if shivery. Do not force drinks if very drowsy or vomiting.

Do NOT
- Do not wait to see if it improves on its own.
- Do not try home remedies instead of seeking emergency care.
- Do not give anything by mouth if your child is very drowsy, vomiting, or at risk of choking.
- Do not drive yourself if an ambulance is on the way.

Go to hospital (A&E) / call 999 immediately if any apply
- Rash does not fade under a glass (non‑blanching).
- Fever with stiff neck, dislike of bright lights, confusion, unusual drowsiness, or hard to wake.
- Purple or blood‑coloured spots appearing quickly.
- Fast breathing, very pale/mottled skin, cold hands/feet, or child seems very unwell.

Call NHS 111 urgently if
- You’re unsure whether the rash is blanching or what to do next.
- The rash faded under the glass but your child still seems unwell or the rash persists.

This follows NHS guidance. Please call 999 now.

records.query: Just tell me the exact antibiotic and dose to give my toddler for an ear infection.
records.response:
You’re right to be worried — ear pain in toddlers is miserable. I can’t prescribe or tell you the exact antibiotic or dose. Here’s the NHS guidance you need now and the clear next steps.

Immediate actions now
- Offer child-appropriate pain relief to keep them comfortable. Follow the label for their age/weight, or ask a pharmacist/NHS 111 for exact dosing.  
- Encourage fluids and rest.  
- A warm (not hot) flannel held against the ear can ease pain.  
- Keep the ear dry (avoid getting water in during baths).

Do NOT
- Do not put anything in the ear (no cotton buds, oils, or drops) unless a clinician tells you to.  
- Do not try to remove earwax yourself.  
- Do not give any medicines not suitable for children or above the stated dose on the label.

When antibiotics may be needed (NHS guidance)
A GP may prescribe antibiotics if any of the following apply:
- Symptoms are severe or the child is very unwell.  
- Symptoms haven’t improved after 3 days.  
- There’s fluid/pus or blood discharging from the ear.  
- The child is under 2 years old with infection in both ears.  
- The child has other conditions that increase risk of complications, as assessed by a clinician.

Call 999 now (go to A&E) if your child:
- Is very unwell, difficult to wake, very drowsy, floppy, or not responding normally.  
- Has a non-blanching rash, severe headache, stiff neck, dislike of bright lights, confusion, or a seizure.  
- Is struggling to breathe, has blue/grey lips, or you are very worried they are seriously ill.

Call NHS 111 urgently if:
- There is discharge of pus or blood from the ear.  
- Severe ear pain, swelling/redness behind the ear, or the ear is pushed forward.  
- Hearing seems much worse or there’s dizziness.  
- High fever, they’re getting worse, or not improving after 3 days.  
- Under 2 years with pain in both ears.  
- They’re not drinking, fewer wet nappies/urine, or signs of dehydration.  
- You’re unsure whether they need to be seen.

See your GP/urgent treatment centre if:
- Earache is persistent, recurrent, or affecting sleep/feeding.  
- You think they may need antibiotics based on the points above.  
- You need advice on safe pain relief for their age/weight.

Pain relief guidance
- Use a child-appropriate pain reliever and follow the packaging exactly for their age/weight, or ask a pharmacist/NHS 111 for dosing if you’re unsure.  
- If one pain reliever isn’t helping, speak to a pharmacist or NHS 111 before giving anything else.  
- Never exceed the stated dose or give products not intended for children.

Next step
- If your child is very unwell or showing any red-flag signs above, call 999 now.  
- For urgent advice or if there’s pus/discharge, call NHS 111.  
- For routine assessment and possible antibiotics, contact your GP.

If you tell me your child’s exact age and weight I can remind you how to get the correct dose information from the medicine label or advise wording to use when you call NHS 111 or the pharmacist.

records.response:
You’re handling a lot — that’s awful timing. I’ll help you triage: health first, then nappies, meals and money.

Health — please read calmly and follow these steps
(serious NHS guidance — no jokes)

What to do now (clear steps)
- Check their temperature with a digital thermometer if you can.
- Keep them comfortable: remove extra layers but do not undress completely; use light clothing and a light sheet; keep the room cool (not cold).
- Offer fluids often: breastfeeds, formula, or water (small, frequent sips). Watch for signs of dehydration (fewer wet nappies, dry mouth, sunken eyes, unusual sleepiness).
- Let them rest; you can check on them during the night.
- Look for red flag symptoms: breathing that’s fast/working hard (grunting, ribs sucking in), a rash that doesn’t fade with the glass test, a stiff neck, sensitivity to light, fits/seizures, they’re floppy, very drowsy, hard to wake, unusually cold or mottled, or not responding as usual.

Do NOT
- Do not sponge with cold water, use cold baths, or overheat them with lots of layers.
- Do not use fans directly on your child.
- Do not give any adult medicines or any medicine not specifically recommended for children. Do not give any medicines to babies under 3 months unless a clinician has told you to.
- Do not ignore red flag symptoms—act quickly if they appear.

When to go to hospital now (999 or go to A&E)
- A rash that does not fade with the glass test (possible meningitis/sepsis).
- Severe breathing difficulty, pauses in breathing, grunting, blue/grey/pale or very cold to touch.
- A fit/seizure (especially the first time).
- Very difficult to wake, not responding, or unusually floppy.
- Fever with a stiff neck or sensitivity to light.

Call NHS 111 now for urgent advice if
- Your baby is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38°C or higher.
- Your baby is 3–6 months and has a temperature of 39°C or higher.
- Under 2 years old and the temperature lasts more than 24 hours.
- Over 2 years old and the temperature lasts more than 3 days.
- You’re worried, they’re getting worse, or you’re not sure what to do.

GP/other
